hyde:
SSH agent forwarding and desktop AI app access: a comment on the security risk.

Yes, it's a real risk. Anything running as your user can talk to the agent socket at SSH_AUTH_SOCK, and the agent will sign challenges for any key it holds without asking you each time. So a compromised or overly permissive app can log into your servers while the agent is unlocked. I'd check whether the app actually needs the socket at all. If not, run it in a sandbox or separate user, or use an agent with confirmation prompts (ssh-add -c, or a hardware key requiring touch). Also avoid forwarding the agent to remote hosts unless you need it.

DNSSEC deployment tradeoffs: a sysadmin's view on whether signing a zone is worth the operational cost.

I run a few dozen zones on Route 53 and BIND, and I turned DNSSEC on for the main domain last year. The signing itself was easy: the registrar and the DNS host both have a checkbox now, and the DS record upload took five minutes. The part that bit us was key rollover. We forgot the KSK rollover date once and a resolver chain started returning SERVFAIL for a few hours. Validation failures are silent for users, so you only hear about them from confused people. If you have someone who will track rollover schedules and monitor for bogus responses, it is worth it. Otherwise I'd skip it for low-value zones.

Revoking unused SSH keys: removing authorized_keys entries, deleting local private keys, and clearing hosted service accounts.

I label every key with a comment at creation, like `ssh-keygen -C "laptop-2019-03"`. Once a year I go through ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on each server, delete anything whose comment I don't recognize, and check the hosts I still use. Removing the public key from authorized_keys is what actually matters; deleting the private key locally is just housekeeping. I also remove the key from GitHub, GitLab, and any cloud console. Keys tied to a lost laptop get revoked immediately, not at audit time.

Security patch delays in Linux distributions and embedded firmware, explaining why a fix that already exists upstream can take weeks to reach users.

I maintained packaging for a mid-sized distro for a few years, and the delay is almost never the fix itself. The upstream patch often lands in a day, but someone then has to backport it onto a version that diverged from main two years ago, and the test suite for that old branch is flaky. The update still has to go through QA and staged rollout, because a bad libc change can break thousands of machines. Embedded vendors are worse. They wait on the chip supplier, who waits on their own release cycle.

Crop wild relatives and heirloom seed lines as sources of disease resistance: the comment argues yes, citing breeders who pull resistance genes back out of old landraces. Written as a first-person HN comment.

Heirloom tomato lines and landraces often carry resistance that modern hybrids lost. Breeders have pulled Fusarium and tobacco mosaic virus resistance out of old varieties and wild Solanum species for decades; the Ty-1 gene for tomato yellow leaf curl virus came from a wild Peruvian relative, not a supermarket cultivar. Modern lines get bred for yield, shelf life, and uniform fruit, and resistance that was not being selected for can quietly drop out. That's why seed banks matter: the resistance is still in the old accessions even when it's gone from commercial seed.

Survivorship bias in stories of sharp nineties-somethings: the comment argues that selection effects and dementia prevalence explain most of the anecdotes.

Mostly yes, though it's two biases stacked. Anecdotes come from people who got interviewed because they were sharp, and the ones with dementia at 91 never get a profile. Dementia prevalence past 85 is roughly a third by most estimates, so a random sample of ninety-year-olds has plenty of people who can't follow the conversation. My grandmother did the crossword at 93, and I only remember it because it was unusual in her nursing home. The real sharp cases do exist, and studies of SuperAgers are interesting, but they're rare outliers, not the typical outcome.

Reliability of ancient DNA as evidence for testing whether origin myths match real population history, based on a researcher's experience with sampling limits.

I did some work on this with a lab collaborator, and ancient DNA is good at showing large movements and mixing over the last few thousand years but weak at confirming any specific story. The sampling is the main problem: you get a few dozen skeletons from a site, and the people the myth describes may have been a small elite whose lineage left no trace. Admixture models also get fitted to the data, so two teams can reach opposite conclusions from the same genomes. I'd treat it as a constraint on the story, not a verdict on it.

Animal model translation to human outcomes in drug trials: the comment argues that mouse results often fail in humans and explains why.

I spent about six years in a preclinical oncology lab, and the mouse-to-human gap is real and mostly boring. Inbred mice are genetically identical and raised in clean, temperature-controlled cages, while patients are heterogeneous and have comorbidities. Tumors implanted in immunodeficient mice also behave differently from the ones that arise in people. The field has cited figures suggesting that a large majority of drugs that work in mice never get approved for humans, though the exact numbers depend on how you count. Mouse studies are still useful for ruling things out and for understanding mechanisms, but I would treat a positive mouse result as a reason to run a human trial, not as evidence the drug works.

Prompted frontier models vs. fine-tuned small models: a comment arguing that large prompted models often win on general tasks, but fine-tuned small models still win on narrow, high-volume tasks with stable formats.

I've gone back and forth on this for a few projects now. For our entity extraction pipeline, a prompted frontier model got us to about 90% accuracy with zero training data, which was great for the first two weeks. But once we had a few thousand labeled examples, a fine-tuned 7B model matched that accuracy, ran about 20x cheaper per call, and had far lower latency. The frontier model was better at odd edge cases nobody had labeled, though. So my rule now: prompt first to find out what the task even is, then fine-tune once the schema is fixed and the volume justifies it.

Argues that loading weights through a Python script still counts as reading them natively, since the heavy lifting happens in compiled code underneath.

Yes, I'd count it, with a caveat. When I run a model with transformers or PyTorch, the weights are read from safetensors or GGUF files by native code. The safetensors loader is Rust, and the matmuls go to CUDA or MKL kernels. Python is mostly orchestration. Calling a hosted API doesn't count, since you never touch the weight bytes. I'd draw the line at whether the file is mmapped and used directly, or whether you parse and convert it yourself in Python.

Share of reinforcement learning in LLM post-training, contrasting SFT-heavy recipes with recent reasoning models trained by RL on verifiable rewards.

Depends what you count. Most open-weight recipes still put the bulk of their data into SFT, with RL as a final stage. The reasoning models shifted that: for R1-style training, RL on verifiable tasks like math and code ate a large share of post-training compute, and labs now talk about RL environments as a major line item. Preference-based RLHF and DPO are a smaller slice than people assume. My guess is RL is a third to half of frontier post-training compute now, but SFT still dominates by data volume.

Cookie consent banners and whether users read them: a commenter's personal experience and reasoning about why people click through.

I'd say almost nobody reads them, and I include myself. Last year I tried to actually go through the options on a banner for a news site I use daily. There were about 140 vendors listed, each with a toggle and a "legitimate interest" switch buried under a second menu. After maybe four minutes I gave up and hit "Accept all," same as everyone. Reading it wasn't really the problem. The design made reading it pointless, since no single person could evaluate that many vendors and the only fast path was the big colorful button.

Malvertising and ad-network exploits as a security reason to run a blocker, not just a preference for less clutter
Yes, and the evidence for this has been pretty clear for years. Malvertising campaigns have repeatedly pushed drive-by exploits through legitimate ad networks, sometimes onto major news sites, with no clicks needed. An ad slot runs third-party JavaScript with access to the page, so a compromised ad server is effectively a compromised site. That attack surface is why I run uBlock Origin. Less clutter and less tracking are nice side effects, but the security argument is what convinced me.

Notifying site owners about a malware infection even when attackers already know about it, and whether staying silent is worth anything.

Yes, tell them. Attackers knowing doesn't mean the owner knows. Last year I found a skimmer on a small bakery's WooCommerce checkout, and the operator had no idea. The malicious script had been sitting in a theme file for months. I emailed the contact on the WHOIS record and got no reply, so I tried the hosting provider. They forwarded it, and the site was cleaned within a day. The people who already know are the ones running the injection, and they aren't going to tell the owner. Silence mostly helps whoever is still scraping card numbers.

Punishing engineers for security mistakes in incident postmortems: the commenter argues blame drives concealment, so blameless reviews and process fixes work better.

Mostly no, and I've seen it backfire. At a previous job, an engineer committed an API key to a repo. The team had a history of punishing people for similar slips, and the second leak came six months later because nobody reported the first near miss until a scanner caught it. When people fear consequences, they stop reporting, and you lose the data you need to find the systemic gap. What worked for us was asking why the key could be committed at all, then adding a pre-commit hook and automated secret scanning.

US AI regulation and migration to Chinese open-weight models: the comment argues that price and capability, not rules, drive adoption, and that compliance costs fall mainly on US hosted services.

Most of the people I know who use Qwen or DeepSeek aren't switching because of regulation. They run them locally or on cheap inference hosts because the weights are free and the quality is good enough for coding and summarization. If US rules only touch hosted APIs from OpenAI or Anthropic, self-hosters won't notice. The risk I'd watch is compliance overhead landing on small US startups, which could make a foreign model the cheaper path for them. Whether that happens depends on how the rules define covered models.

Open-weight model licensing vs. hosting business economics: a commenter argues that openness matters less than who controls serving costs and ops.

Yes, but mostly as a pricing question. We run a small inference product on an open-weight model, and the weights being open saved us from a vendor lock-in negotiation, which was worth a lot. But the moment we had to sell it, the real problems were GPU utilization, cold starts, and support tickets about latency spikes. Nobody pays for "open." They pay for a reliable endpoint with a clear SLA. Openness lowers your cost of entry and gives you a fallback if a provider raises prices, but it doesn't replace having the ops to run it.

H-1B visa policy and offshoring as causes of US tech layoffs: a commenter's view on whether they explain tech unemployment.

I don't think H-1B or offshoring explain most of the tech unemployment we've seen. When my team got cut last year, the roles that disappeared were mostly the ones tied to the 2021-2022 hiring boom: recruiters, growth marketing, and internal tooling teams that existed because money was cheap. The offshore work I've seen was usually maintenance or QA that was already overseas. H-1B people I've worked with were often the ones kept on because they were expensive to lose on a sponsored visa. Rates and interest policy seemed to matter far more than either program.

Anthropic's debt exposure if revenue growth slows: the comment argues its main obligations are multi-year cloud compute commitments rather than bonds, so the risk is mostly contractual.

As far as I know Anthropic has very little traditional debt, so the question is less about bondholders and more about what it has already promised to pay. The big line items are compute contracts with cloud providers, which are often multi-year minimum spend commitments. If revenue growth stalls while those commitments are locked in, the squeeze shows up as a cash burn problem rather than a default on loans. Equity raises cover the gap for now, but investors price that in, so a slowdown would make the next round the real test.

Share of AI-linked companies in S&P 500 index funds, based on cap-weighted top holdings.

Depends how you define AI, but for an S&P 500 or total-market fund the exposure is bigger than most people expect. Nvidia alone was around 7% of the index the last time I checked, and Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Broadcom and Oracle add several more points between them. Counting those, you're probably somewhere around 20-30% of the fund. Open your fund's holdings page, sort by weight, and pick which names you'd call AI. The number shifts every quarter because these stocks have run up and the index is cap-weighted.

Whether Anthropic's disclosed filings show its real compute spending, given that the s1 paper doesn't address it.

Neither, as far as I can tell. The s1 paper is about fine-tuning a reasoning model on about 1,000 examples and using budget forcing at test time. It reports GPU hours for its own small training run, nothing about Anthropic. Anthropic also hasn't published an S-1 with audited compute costs. The figures you see quoted as their actual spend usually come from press reports or investor materials, so I'd treat them as estimates.

Consumer subscription versus API revenue for AI labs, arguing that subscriptions are predictable but fragile while API revenue is lumpier but stickier.

I think it depends on what you mean by safer. Subscriptions give predictable monthly cash, but churn is brutal once a free tier gets good enough, and a competitor's cheaper plan can empty a cohort in one quarter. API revenue is lumpier and more concentrated, but it's usually tied to a product a customer has already built on top of you. Switching costs are real when someone has prompts, evals, and retry logic tuned to your model. Both get hit when the underlying model gets commoditized, so I'd look at gross margin on each before deciding.

Vendor support forums' usefulness for troubleshooting: the commenter argues they were often helpful for obscure driver and firmware bugs.
Honestly, yes, for a while they were the best place to get answers. Around 2008 I spent a week stuck on a RAID controller that kept dropping a disk under load. The official phone support just told me to reflash. A forum thread from a guy in another country had the actual fix: a specific firmware revision plus a registry tweak for the write cache timeout. Engineers from the vendor sometimes posted directly, which made a big difference. The signal faded once vendors moved to ticket portals and reddit-style spam filters buried everything.

Jailbreaking aftermarket Android car head units: this comment weighs the payoff of rooting them against the risks and limited upside.

I did this on a cheap Android head unit last year. Rooting got me a working ADB shell and let me swap the launcher and kill the ads in the bundled nav app, which was nice. But the stock firmware was a mess and the root exploit was tied to one build, so an OTA update would have bricked the root. The real win was reflashing the Chinese firmware to fix the GPS drift. If you just want Android Auto or CarPlay, buy a unit that has it. Otherwise it's a weekend of fun, not a daily upgrade.

Style guide rules on writing versus language standards: a commenter's take on how strictly to follow grammar conventions.

I'd follow them strictly in anything meant for strangers to read, like docs, error messages, and commit messages, because those readers can't ask what you meant. Outside that, I think the rules are tools. I used to chase every "whom" and comma splice in internal wikis until a senior engineer pointed out that nobody was confused, they were just annoyed. Now I ask whether a rule prevents a misreading or just signals education. If it prevents confusion, I follow it. If it's a shibboleth, I break it on purpose and accept that some people will judge me for it.

Anthropomorphizing LLMs in discussions of "thinking," "understanding," and "wanting": this comment argues the vocabulary matters less than whether it leads to wrong predictions.

I think the answer is yes, but I'd push back on treating it as purely a wording problem. Saying a model "wants" something is shorthand that's fine until you start designing around it, like assuming it will respect an instruction the way a coworker would. The useful test for me is whether the metaphor changes what you expect it to do next. If "it thinks the code is correct" leads you to skip tests, that's the mistake. If you're just using it as a compact way to say "the output is conditioned on the prompt," the shorthand costs nothing. Most of the confusion I've seen comes from people never making that distinction explicit.

Self-taught programmers and whether a CS degree is needed for strong engineering work: the commenter describes their own path and what they think mattered.

I dropped out of a non-CS degree and learned programming by building things for a small logistics company. Nobody checked whether I knew what a B-tree was. What I did learn the hard way was debugging, reading other people's code, and writing tests that caught my mistakes. Years later I went back and read algorithms and operating systems material, mostly because I kept hitting problems where the theory explained why my code fell over. I think you can be very good without the degree, but you usually fill those gaps eventually, and the gaps show up in hiring and in tough design work.

Arecibo's 2020 collapse, and the claim that the observatory's own radio transmissions caused it.

No. The NSF investigation traced the collapse to a mechanical failure. A main cable that held the platform slipped out of its socket at the tower, and the platform came down as the load shifted to the other cables. Inspections had flagged broken wires and worn sockets in those cables for years. Radio energy aimed at the sky doesn't put meaningful stress on a steel and concrete structure, so the radio explanation confuses the telescope's work with the cable problems that were documented long before the fall.

Arecibo's transmit capability, including the 1974 message and planetary radar work, shows it sent signals as well as receiving them.

Both. The famous 1974 Arecibo message was beamed from the 305 m dish at about 2380 MHz toward the M13 star cluster, using a transmitter of roughly a megawatt. The more routine sending work was planetary radar: the dish fired high-power pulses at Venus, Mercury, and near-Earth asteroids, then listened for the echoes to map their surfaces and refine their orbits. That's why it was a radar facility, not just a receiver. Most of its time went to passive astronomy, but the transmitter was a core part of the observatory.

Claude generating interface prototypes as HTML/CSS without Figma or similar tools: a commenter's experience with that workflow.

I've been doing this for a few months and it works better than I expected. I ask for a single HTML file with inline CSS, a fixed set of screens, and clickable nav with plain JS, then open it in the browser and iterate by pasting screenshots back in. Layout and spacing are usually close on the first pass. Where it struggles is consistent design tokens across many screens, so I ask for CSS variables up front. For stakeholder reviews, a clickable HTML mock beats static Figma frames anyway. You lose the component library and auto-layout, though, so it's not great if your team hands off to engineers through Figma.

Custom-drawn web UIs on canvas or with div-based widgets, and the native browser behaviors they lose, such as accessibility, find-in-page, and form autofill.

Most of it, in my experience. When I rebuilt a dashboard on canvas, Ctrl+F stopped finding anything, because the text isn't in the DOM. Screen readers saw an empty page until we added a hidden ARIA mirror, and even then tab order was wrong. Right-click menus, copy-paste formatting, and print layout all changed too. Autofill and password managers couldn't see the inputs we drew. Zoom and high-contrast mode broke because we hardcoded pixel sizes. We ended up reimplementing about half of what the browser gave us for free, and users noticed the gaps more than the pretty parts.

AI coding assistants' effect on programmer employment: a first-person take on whether they augment or replace developers.

I've been using Copilot and Claude daily for about two years on a mid-sized backend team. For boilerplate, test scaffolding, and migrating old API clients they save real time, maybe a few hours a week. But the work that takes the longest is still figuring out what the product should do and why production broke at 2am, and the tool doesn't touch that. What I have seen is that our junior hiring slowed down, and I think that's the part people should worry about. If seniors can do more with the same headcount, the pipeline that trains the next seniors gets thinner.

AI coding assistants trade-off between speed and code quality
 
I've shipped a few projects with Copilot and Claude over the last year, and my experience is that speed gains are real but quality drops unless I'm strict about review. The code runs and passes the happy-path tests, but I keep finding duplicated helpers, error handling that swallows exceptions, and abstractions nobody asked for. Reviewing a generated 300-line diff takes longer than I'd like, and I've caught subtle bugs only after they hit staging. When I write small functions myself and let the model fill in boilerplate, quality holds up. So it's less that AI sacrifices quality by default and more that it removes the friction that used to force careful thinking.

Verifiable AI discoveries such as AlphaTensor's matrix multiplication scheme, FunSearch's cap sets, and AlphaDev's sorting routines.

Yes, I'd point to a few that hold up. AlphaTensor (DeepMind, 2022) found a 47-multiplication scheme for multiplying two 4x4 matrices over GF(2), beating Strassen's 49 from 1969, and you can check the scheme by expanding it yourself. FunSearch (2023) produced larger cap sets in dimension 8 than were previously known, and the programs it wrote are readable. AlphaDev's sort routines for small arrays were verified and merged into LLVM's libc++. The caveat is that these are narrow problems where candidates can be scored automatically, so I wouldn't call it general discovery.

Proposals to tax AI-generated code would likely target compute or API usage rather than the software itself, which is hard to define and enforce.

I doubt it. A tax on "all software written" would need a definition of "written" that holds up against autocomplete, linters, and code generators that have existed for decades, and nobody has one. The more plausible version is a levy on metered API usage or inference compute, which AI vendors already track to the cent. That hits whoever runs models at scale, not the person typing a shell script. We saw the same pattern with cloud egress fees: the bill follows the meter, not the artifact. So I'd expect taxes on tokens or GPUs long before anything touches the output.

AI involvement in recent aviation IT outages, such as the 2024 CrowdStrike and 2023 FAA NOTAM failures, with the commenter finding no public evidence that AI caused either.

I haven't seen any evidence that AI was involved in the aviation outages I'm aware of. The big one was CrowdStrike's faulty Falcon sensor update in July 2024, which crashed Windows machines and grounded flights at several airlines. The FAA's NOTAM system failure in January 2023 was traced to a contractor accidentally deleting files during a database update. Both have documented, human-process causes in their post-incident reports. If someone is claiming AI was responsible, I'd want to see a postmortem that says so, because nothing I've read does.

Airline ground-stop outage debate: a commenter argues that the failure reflects procurement, testing, and deadline decisions more than programmers' competence.

I doubt it says much about programmers in general. I worked on crew scheduling software for a regional carrier, and the problems we shipped came from skipped load testing, a single database nobody was allowed to fail over, and launch dates set by sales. The engineers I worked with were careful, but they were told to ship before the migration had been tested. Much of this software is also decades old and patched in layers. Outages like this are usually a chain of decisions, and one bad line is rarely the root cause.

Aviation outage sabotage versus ordinary failure, and which evidence would distinguish them: correlated timing, access logs, and backup-path status.

Possible, but I'd check the boring explanations first. Most large outages in systems like this come from a bad config push or an expired certificate that cascades. What would make me suspect something else is failures appearing in separately hosted systems within the same minute, or unauthorized logins or changes shortly before. I'd also want to know whether the backup paths failed too, since a deliberate attack often targets redundancy. Without those signals, I'd assume a change-management problem until proven otherwise.

Hobbyist dashboards that combined FAA airport status feeds with scheduled-flight data to show which airports were losing flights during the 2025 government shutdown.

I threw together a script that polls the FAA status data every few minutes, logs which airports had ground delay or ground stop entries, and compares that against scheduled departures from a flight data API. It showed the cuts were concentrated at the big hubs rather than spread evenly. A few people built map versions that color-coded airports by how many scheduled flights were missing. The hard part wasn't the code. The official numbers lagged and the schedule data had gaps, so I had to label the output as estimates.

Running local LLMs on older Nvidia GPUs like the GTX 1080 Ti and RTX 2060, with measured tokens-per-second for quantized 7B and 13B models.

I ran a 1080 Ti (11GB) for a while with llama.cpp. A Q4_K_M 7B model fit entirely in VRAM and gave about 45 tokens/sec for generation, while prompt processing was in the few-hundred tokens/sec range. A 13B Q4 model still fit but got around 25 t/s. Once the model spilled into system RAM, speed dropped to maybe 5 t/s, which was painful. Pascal lacks tensor cores, so FP16 paths are slow, but quantized inference works fine. A 2060 with 6GB was limited to 7B at Q4 with short context.

Consumer versus enterprise pricing for high-core-count CPUs and AI accelerators, arguing that general compute remains affordable while only top GPUs are business-focused.

Not really, at least for general compute. A Threadripper or a used EPYC box gets you 64 cores for a few thousand dollars, which is less than many people spend on a car. What has changed is the top GPU tier. H100-class cards are mostly sold to data centers, and consumer cards were capped on memory and multi-GPU support. I bought a used Xeon workstation last year for under $800, and it builds my projects faster than my laptop ever did. The gap is real for accelerators, but for CPUs and RAM it's still a normal hobbyist purchase.

DDR5 desktop RAM price spikes and whether they're pushing home PC upgrades out of reach, as told by a builder comparing kit costs.

I just priced a 2x32GB DDR5 kit for a home build, and it's about double what I paid last year. The bigger issue for me is that I already have 32GB, so the upgrade I planned is now a wait-and-see situation. I'd rather not spend that on memory while my current box handles everything I throw at it. On older boards that can't take DDR5, the math is worse because you'd have to replace the whole platform. I'm holding off until prices settle.

Heavy quantization of local LLMs to 2–4 bits, describing how much output quality drops compared with fp16 weights based on the commenter's own tests.

In my testing on a 70B model, Q4_K_M was hard to tell apart from fp16 in normal chat, but the gap showed up in multi-step math and long code edits. Q3 was where I started noticing it: more dropped constraints and occasional wrong variable names after a few thousand tokens. Q2 was rough. It stayed fluent but would confidently invent APIs. Perplexity numbers understate this a bit, since the errors are rare per token but cluster on exactly the tasks people care about. My rule now: 4-bit is the floor for anything I'd trust unattended.

Running several AI coding agents in parallel: how one developer tracks their tasks, branches, and output.

I run each agent in its own git worktree with a separate branch, so they can't step on each other's files. I keep a plain TODO.md at the repo root with one line per task, its branch, and its status, and each agent updates its own line when it finishes. A tmux session has a pane per agent that tails its log, so I can see who's stuck without switching windows. The part that still bites me is review. Once more than three agents are going, I fall behind on diffs, so I now cap it at three and only start a new one when a finished branch is merged.

Multiple AI coding agents running in parallel: whether they raise real throughput or just add review overhead.

I ran three coding agents at once on a refactor across our billing service for about two weeks. The first week was a mess. They kept touching the same files, and I spent more time resolving merge conflicts and re-reading diffs than I saved. What worked was splitting work by module with strict file ownership, and only running a second agent when the task was clearly independent. Now I usually run two. The gain is real but smaller than the demos suggest, and it mostly comes from the agents doing tedious test-writing while I review something else. Review time is the actual bottleneck, so a third bot without a third set of eyes just produces more code to check.

Local LLM hardware for offline coding assistants: the comment describes a specific machine and model setup.

I run a Qwen2.5-Coder 32B quantized to Q4 through llama.cpp on an M2 Max MacBook Pro with 64GB of unified memory. It fits comfortably and generates around 12 tokens per second, which is fine for autocomplete-style suggestions and chat. For tab completion I use the 7B variant since latency matters more than quality there. On a desktop I tried a used RTX 3090 with 24GB VRAM and it was faster, but the 32B model barely fit with a short context. If you're on a budget, a 16GB card running a 14B model is a reasonable middle ground. Memory bandwidth matters more than raw compute for token generation, so I'd prioritize that when choosing hardware.

OpenRouter pricing versus flat-rate AI subscriptions comparison

I've used both for about six months. For light use, OpenRouter wins: I paid maybe $12 total for a few hundred Claude and GPT-4o queries, and nothing sitting unused. Heavy daily coding is different. Once I was sending long context through Sonnet every day, the per-token bill went past the $20 subscription fast, and the subscription was the cheaper option. My rule now is that if you use it under an hour a day, go pay-as-you-go. Otherwise the flat plan is the better deal.

Huang's alleged lying and his affairs: which one does more damage to trust in his work?
I'd say the lying was worse, mainly because it reached people who had no say in his personal life. An affair is a private breach, and most of us can judge it without knowing much about the business. Lying to investors, board members, or staff about facts they used to make decisions is different. If the denials were false and people relied on them when they put money or jobs on the line, that's a much bigger problem than the affairs alone.

Whether Jensen Huang leaving Nvidia as CEO could burst the AI bubble, with the commenter arguing the real risk is hyperscaler capex and financing, not one person.

I doubt it. Huang is very good at selling, but most of the demand comes from Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta spending something like a couple hundred billion a year on data centers. If he left tomorrow, those orders would mostly still happen, because the buyers judge by their own model roadmaps, not his stage presence. The fragile part is the financing: a lot of that spending is backed by debt, circular deals with startups, and GPU-backed loans. A CEO change might move the stock a lot, but I'd watch depreciation schedules and whether inference revenue actually shows up.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's health and availability matter to investors because the company depends heavily on his judgment about product bets and supply deals, which makes key-person risk material.

Mostly because Nvidia is a founder-led company, and Huang's calls on product bets and supply deals are hard to replace. If he were out for a few months, the stock could move a lot, so anything that affects his availability is material, not gossip. Investors also look at whether the board has a succession plan and whether he has disclosed one. His share sales under 10b5-1 plans get scrutiny for the same reason. None of this means his family or hobbies matter, just his availability and incentives.

Speculation over whether the Huang corruption scandal was a politically motivated hit job to push him out of his party.

I followed this closely at the time, and I don't think the timing alone proves much. The charges came out of a prosecutor's office that had been investigating his former aide for over a year, and the documents that surfaced were mostly bank records, not the speeches people keep quoting. That said, the leak to the press landed about three weeks before the party primary, and that's the part I'd want explained. If you want to settle it, look at who had access to the sealed filings rather than at the verdict.

Alternatives to systemd as Linux init: runit, OpenRC, s6, and SysV init, plus Devuan and Alpine as distros that use them.
 
Alternatives to systemd as Linux init and service manager: runit, OpenRC, s6, and SysV init.

I ran Void on a couple of laptops for about three years, and runit has been the least annoying init I've used. Services are just directories with a run script, so debugging means reading a shell file instead of a binary journal. Supervision works well: if a daemon dies, runsv restarts it. The downside is that you lose a lot of the desktop glue systemd gives you for free, like logind and some socket activation, so you end up installing separate pieces for suspend handling and user sessions. OpenRC is the choice if you want dependency ordering and still prefer plain scripts, which is why Alpine and Gentoo use it.

AI-assisted vulnerability scanning of open source code: the comment describes personal experience using an LLM to review dependencies and code for security issues.

I ran an LLM over a few mid-sized open source projects last month, mostly Python and Go, and it was useful but noisy. It caught a real path traversal in a file upload handler and flagged an unsafe YAML load that static tools had missed. It also produced a lot of false positives, like calling sanitized inputs unsanitized. What worked best was pairing it with semgrep and a fuzzer: the model triaged findings and wrote candidate exploit inputs, and the fuzzer confirmed them. I wouldn't trust it as the only reviewer, but as a second pass on a codebase nobody has audited, it found things a human skimming the diff would likely skip.

Ubuntu kernel fix delivery delays from downstream patch carrying, ABI stability rules, and SRU testing across several kernel flavors, explained from experience.

Mostly because you're maintaining a fork, not applying a patch. Ubuntu's kernel is upstream plus several hundred downstream patches, so a clean upstream fix often conflicts and needs manual rebasing. The ABI is another constraint: you can't change struct layouts to fix a bug without breaking modules built against that release. Each fix then goes through an SRU process and gets tested across GA, HWE, cloud, and OEM kernels that share code but not config. I've seen a one-line change take three weeks for that reason.

Arch Linux maintenance burden and whether it requires constant tinkering
A rolling release means updates arrive continuously, but I'd push back on the idea that it's constant fiddling. I've run Arch on my laptop for about four years. Most months, pacman -Syu goes through without a single prompt. The breakage I've hit came maybe three times, and each was a known issue listed on the Arch news page before I updated. I read that page before big upgrades and it has saved me. My desktop has needed zero manual intervention in the last year. The setup phase is where the real work is, and after that it's mostly quiet.

Spotting bot comments on forums by checking account age, posting cadence, and generic phrasing

A few things I look at. A fresh account that jumps straight into long, confident replies on random threads is suspicious. I also check the history for posting rhythm, like dozens of comments within minutes around the clock, or replies that never engage with the specific point of the article. The tell I trust most is the generic summary that could be pasted under any post on the topic. Real people usually mention some oddly specific detail, or they're wrong in a way that's clearly theirs.

AI-generated websites lowering trust in a product: a personal take on whether a generic-looking landing page makes a developer hesitate.
 
I'd say yes, but mostly as a shortcut for something else. When I land on a SaaS page with the stock gradient hero, vague "seamless, powerful, next-gen" copy, and identical feature cards, I assume nobody on the team cared enough to say anything specific about what the product does. That's the real signal. I've bounced from tools that were probably great because the docs had no real screenshots and the changelog was empty. If the site is AI-made but the pricing is clear, the limits are documented, and the error messages are honest, I stop caring how it was built.

AI training data opt-outs and whether to stop posting publicly: a commenter weighs the tradeoff and argues that posting is still worth it for most people.

I don't think going silent is the right move for most people. Anything you posted before the scraping started is already out there, and pulling it now mostly just removes your name from places people search. I'd focus on things you can actually control: check whether a platform offers an opt-out or a data-download setting, avoid putting anything sensitive like contracts, medical details, or private photos in public text, and use a separate account for stuff you don't want tied to your real identity. Writing still helped me more than any training run ever will, since the people I've met through blog posts and HN comments are the reason I keep doing it.

AI-generated indie games on Steam: whether rough, low-polish releases still find an audience worth the effort of shipping.

I shipped a small puzzle game last year with AI-generated sprites and placeholder music, and it sold about 400 copies in the first month. Most of the negative reviews were about the art, but the people who bought it mostly said the core loop was fun. Refunds were around 8%, which was higher than my other project. I'd say it's still worth releasing if the mechanic works and you don't expect it to pay rent. The real cost now is discoverability, since Steam gets flooded with similar titles every week.

AI-assisted game development for hobbyists: a commenter describes using an LLM to write Godot scripts and make placeholder assets, and where it still falls short.

Yes, for the boring parts. Last month I built a small 2D platformer in Godot with almost no prior game experience. I'd describe a state machine or an inventory system to a chat model and it gave me a working GDScript skeleton I could debug in an afternoon. It was also useful for placeholder sprites and sound effects I could swap out later. Where it failed was anything involving physics feel or camera behavior; the model kept suggesting fixes that looked right but made the jump feel floaty. Still, feel takes hand tuning.

Reviving old game ports runs into lost source code, dead toolchains, and expired middleware licenses, and this comment lists those problems from a personal attempt.

I tried porting a 2001 Windows shooter last year and the source was on a backup tape that was unreadable. We ended up decompiling the release binary, which took weeks. The build used a compiler that no longer exists, so I had to reconstruct the project file by hand. The audio middleware license had lapsed, and the vendor no longer answers email. Save files depended on struct padding from 32-bit MSVC, so they broke on 64-bit builds. Many of the bugs only showed up at resolutions the original team never tested.

Retro 8-bit game development in the 1980s, personal experience with coding for Commodore 64 and Atari machines.
The biggest constraint was memory. On a C64 you had about 38K free in BASIC, so we wrote the core loop in 6502 assembly and kept everything else tight. Sprites were limited to eight per line, so flicker was a constant fight. Graphics were usually defined in a tiny grid of characters, and you planned level layouts on graph paper because there was no room for editors. Debugging meant a machine code monitor and a lot of staring at the screen. Cassette loading took minutes, and a single typo could crash everything. It was painful, but the limits forced clever tricks that still shape how I design code today.

Rust's compiler guarantees for memory safety and how they bear on whether AI-generated code can be trusted without line-by-line review.

Partly. The borrow checker rules out use-after-free and data races, which are the bugs LLMs produce most quietly in C and C++. But it says nothing about whether the code does what you wanted. I have had Claude write Rust that compiles, passes the type checker, and still clamps a negative timestamp to zero because it misread the spec. The compiler catches the bugs that are easiest to miss by hand, so you can review less for memory issues, but logic review and tests still carry the weight. Rust makes bad code fail louder, not correct.

Slint's .slint markup language versus Rust, and whether a Slint interface counts as writing the UI in Rust.

Not really, the markup is a separate language. Slint UIs are declared in .slint files, which look a bit like CSS mixed with property bindings. A build.rs step (slint-build) compiles those into Rust code, and you wire callbacks and properties up from normal Rust. So the app logic and glue are all Rust, but the layout is a second DSL. If you want the whole interface in Rust with no second language, egui or iced are the closer fit. I used Slint for a small settings panel and the split felt clean.

Rust compile-time improvements like the LLD default linker, the parallel frontend, and Cranelift, and how they move to stable releases

The LLD linker became the default on x86_64 Linux in stable releases last year, which cut link times on our large workspace. The parallel frontend is still behind -Zthreads on nightly, and the Cranelift backend is an opt-in nightly component, so those will take longer to stabilize since they touch compiler internals. My rule of thumb: anything that changes codegen output or default flags goes through a long beta period, so expect incremental wins to land in point releases and the bigger ones to take a year or more.

Lisp adoption in big companies: a skeptical take on whether famous examples show wide use. The comment argues that a handful of prominent users does not establish broad adoption.

I'd push back on treating a few famous names as proof. Yes, Jane Street, Grammarly, and ITA Software (later Google) shipped serious Lisp or Lisp-family code, but those are headline cases from a much larger industry. When I worked at a mid-sized firm, we looked at Common Lisp for a backend and dropped it because hiring was hard and the library ecosystem was thin. Companies that use Lisp tend to be unusually small teams with unusually strong hiring pipelines. The better question is what share of production code, or what number of job postings, is Lisp. By that measure it's a niche language, even if the examples are impressive.

Lisp vs. Haskell learning curve: the comment argues Lisp's tiny syntax is quicker to start with, while Haskell's type system and purity make the early days harder.

I think Lisp is easier to get started with, mostly because there's almost no syntax. You learn parens, prefix calls, and a handful of special forms, and you can write useful code in a weekend. Haskell front-loads a lot more: laziness, type classes, monads, and the compiler errors that come with them. But the difficulty shifts. Lisp gets hard later when you need macros and good design habits, while Haskell's wall is at the beginning and then flattens out. If you want to be productive fast, Lisp wins. If you want the type checker to catch your mistakes, Haskell pays back the effort.

AI-generated code for long-lived projects: a comment giving a practical opinion on maintainability.

AI-written code maintainability for long-lived projects: a comment arguing it works if you review and own every line, but suffers when generated code is merged unread.

I've used Copilot and Claude on a service we've kept running for about six years, and my take is that the code itself isn't the problem, unreviewed code is. The generated stuff tends to be verbose, repeats helpers that already exist elsewhere in the repo, and makes up plausible-looking library calls that don't match the version we pin. Those bugs show up a year later when nobody remembers why a function exists. What works for us: tests written first, small diffs, and a rule that whoever commits the code can explain every branch in it.

Racket's macro system as a way to implement custom type rules as ordinary library code, with Typed Racket as the example.

Yes, mostly, and Racket is the cleanest example I've used. Macros run at compile time as ordinary Racket functions over syntax objects, so you can write a checker that walks the program and rejects what it doesn't like. Typed Racket works this way: it's a library that installs its own type checker and then hands the result back to the normal compiler. The limit is that you can't change how the core evaluator treats things, only what gets through to it. In Lisp terms, the type rules are just code.

Ubuntu's snap packages and default desktop complaints: a comment griping about slow snap app startup and the Amazon search integration.

I keep hitting the same three annoyances on Ubuntu. Snaps are the biggest one for me: Firefox and Chromium take several seconds to launch because the squashfs mount has to spin up, and apt quietly installing a snap stub instead of the real package still bugs me. Then there's the Ubuntu desktop itself, where the dock eats screen space and GNOME extensions break after every upgrade. Last, the release cadence and LTS upgrades have burned me more than once when a driver or a PPA stopped working. None of this makes it unusable, but it's why I end up on Debian or Fedora for workstations.

AI bubble discourse: a commenter's take on whether current AI valuations and capex look like the dot-com bust in the making.

I think we're in a bubble, but not the kind that pops and erases the technology. Nvidia's margins and the hyperscaler capex numbers only make sense if every company ends up paying for inference at scale, and I haven't seen the revenue to back that up yet. I worked at a company that bought GPU capacity in 2023 on a promise of demand that never showed up, and we spent most of 2024 quietly downsizing it. The models are useful, though. The part I'd bet against is the valuations assuming that usefulness converts to margins for the people currently raising billions.

Coding agents in daily use: Claude Code, Cursor, Aider, Codex CLI, and how they compare in practice.
Been using Claude Code for about four months on a mid-sized Rails app, mostly for refactors and writing tests for legacy code. It handles multi-file changes well if I give it a clear spec up front. I still use Cursor when I want to stay in the editor and tweak things by hand. Aider was my first agent and I like its git integration, but I moved off it because it needed more hand-holding on larger tasks. I haven't settled on Codex CLI yet; it feels fast but I trust its edits less so far.

Jensen Huang's reputation among developers and investors, covering his CUDA bet, management style, and criticism of AI hype.

I think he's one of the better CEOs of the last twenty years. Betting on CUDA in 2006, when almost nobody wanted GPU compute, and funding it through years of thin returns is not something most execs would have stuck with. He also runs Nvidia with a famously flat structure and a lot of direct reports, which works for him. My main complaint is the hype. Some of the "AI will do X" talk runs ahead of what the products actually deliver.

Rust developer sentiment and the tradeoffs of adopting it: a personal take on the learning curve versus payoff.

I've written Rust professionally for about three years, and my feelings have shifted from frustration to genuine affection. The borrow checker fought me for the first few months, and I won't pretend otherwise. But once it clicked, I stopped spending time on whole classes of bugs I used to chase in Go and C++. Refactoring large codebases without fear is the real win for me. The compile times still hurt on big projects, and async ergonomics are rough. Still, I'd pick it again for anything long-lived.

AI-generated code objections on HN: a comment listing the common objections, first person.

Common objections to AI-written code, as a comment about reviewing LLM output in a team codebase: the note should start with the specific topic, e.g., "Objections to AI-written code in production, mainly review burden, subtle bugs, and licensing."

Comment draft (40-100 words), first person, concrete.

Let me write it.

Objections to AI-written code in production, mainly review burden, subtle bugs, and maintainability concerns.

I keep hearing the same three complaints from our reviewers. First, the diffs are huge and plausible-looking, so reviewing them takes longer than writing the code would have. Second, the bugs are the quiet kind: an off-by-one in a retry loop, or a hallucinated library flag that compiles but does nothing. Third, nobody on the team can explain why a block exists, so it becomes untouchable. I don't think these are fatal, but they're real costs, and "the model wrote it" is not a justification in a postmortem.

Home local LLM setups for consumer GPUs and Apple Silicon: a commenter lists the open-weight models they run and the hardware behind them.

I run Qwen2.5 14B at Q4_K_M on a 3090 through llama.cpp, which fits fully in 24GB and gets around 35 tokens/sec. For coding help I switched to Qwen2.5-Coder 32B at Q4, which just squeezes in and is noticeably slower at around 15 tok/s. On a 64GB M2 Max I've been running Llama 3.1 70B at Q4 through Ollama, usable but sluggish. Mistral Nemo 12B is my go-to for quick summaries because it's fast and light. Anything under 7B feels too dumb for my taste.

Expectations and speculation about PostgreSQL 20, noting that the version isn't released yet and what users hope it includes.

PostgreSQL 20 isn't out yet. The project ships one major version a year, so on that cadence it would land around autumn 2027. I've seen people mention wanting better logical replication for major upgrades, native sharding, and built-in connection pooling, but most of that is wishlist talk rather than committed work. Honestly, I'd wait for the beta notes before planning anything around it. Our team is still on 16, and that's working fine for us.

Arecibo Observatory's rebuild status: the comment says no rebuild is underway because NSF decided against restoring the collapsed 305-meter dish.

Short answer: it isn't. After the cable failures in 2020 and the collapse of the platform into the dish that December, NSF ran an environmental review and in late 2021 decided not to rebuild the telescope. The money was redirected to other radio astronomy projects. What's left at the site is mostly cleanup, decommissioning, and the visitor center. Some people in Puerto Rico still push for a restored dish, but I haven't seen a funded plan for one. For current details, the NSF announcements and the University of Central Florida's observatory updates are the places I'd check.

Jensen Huang's leadership at Nvidia, which he has led since co-founding the company in 1993, in a thread about the CEO.

There's no new Nvidia CEO as far as I know. Jensen has run the company since he co-founded it in 1993, so if you saw a headline about someone new, it may have been about a different role or a different company. Opinions on him are mixed. Many people credit him with betting early on CUDA, which paid off hugely when deep learning took off. Others criticize Nvidia's pricing power and the tight supply of data center chips. I'd check the source of whatever prompted the question.

The January 2023 FAA NOTAM system outage and its effect on European airports, mainly through transatlantic flight delays.

Not directly. The NOTAM failure was a US system, so Heathrow, Frankfurt and Schiphol kept running their own airspace as normal. The knock-on was on transatlantic flights: the FAA halted departures to US airports for a few hours, so a number of flights from Europe were held at the gate or cancelled, and some arrived late. I was checking flight status from Dublin that morning and saw a pile of delays on the US-bound boards, but nothing on the European side itself. Most of those delays were cleared by evening.

CoreWeave's March 2025 Nasdaq IPO, priced at $40 a share and raising roughly $1.5 billion, below the originally marketed range.

I read through the pricing announcement when it came out. CoreWeave priced at $40 a share, under the $47 to $55 range it had first marketed, and sold about 37.5 million shares, so the gross raise was around $1.5 billion. That's well below the earlier chatter. The valuation at pricing was roughly $23 billion. Keep in mind that's before underwriting fees. Most of the cash was earmarked for general corporate purposes, including paying down debt and funding data center buildout, so the IPO was a small piece of the capital they've been raising overall.

Speculation about Ubuntu 28.04 LTS, noting that the release is years away and focusing on whether Canonical keeps its LTS cadence and support window.

Honestly, most of what I've seen is speculation, since 28.04 is still years out and the schedule could change. The recurring question is whether Canonical keeps the two-year LTS rhythm and the five-year standard support window. Some people also wonder whether 28.04 will drop older hardware or change the installer. Our fleet depends on that support window, so we're staying on 24.04 and will judge later releases on their point-release track record.

Blender 6 upgrade advice: a commenter says no Blender 6 release is known to them, and recommends staying on the current 4.x or 5.x line and waiting for a point release.

As far as I know there's no Blender 6 release yet, so check the official site before planning anything. Most people's version numbers are still 4.x or 5.x, and I'd stay on the current stable build for production work. Major releases tend to break Python add-ons and change some shader or geometry nodes behavior, so I wait for the .1 or .2 point release, then test my own scene files in a copy before switching. If your work depends on specific add-ons, check their support pages first. Upgrading is worth it when a feature you need actually lands, not just because it's new.

Rust on RISC-V laptops: official riscv64gc Linux toolchains work well, but native compile speed and occasional crate build-script breakage are the main pain points.

I've been daily-driving a VisionFive 2 for about a year, and Rust mostly just works. rustup ships riscv64gc-unknown-linux-gnu builds, so cargo install and small projects are painless. The catch is speed: something that takes 40 seconds on my x86 machine takes six or seven minutes on its four cores, and 8GB of RAM means big link steps can swap. Crates with C dependencies or hand-written assembly sometimes need patches, and I've hit a few build scripts that assumed x86. For anything serious, cross-compiling from a faster host is the sensible workflow.

Claude Code on Windows: a commenter finds native install workable with Git Bash, but says WSL2 is smoother because of shell and path quirks.

I've used it on Windows 11 for about two months. Native install was painless once I had Git for Windows, since it wants Git Bash for its shell tool. Where it bit me was PowerShell: commands it generated assumed bash syntax, and it occasionally tried paths that broke. Switching to WSL2 fixed most of that, but then file watching on /mnt/c got slow for big repos, so I keep the repo inside the Linux filesystem. Overall it's usable on Windows, but expect to fight the shell more than you would on macOS.

Discord's Rust rewrite of the read-states service and whether it affected voice chat
As far as I know, the Rust rewrite didn't touch voice. It replaced the Go read-states service, mainly to get rid of the periodic latency spikes from garbage collection. Voice runs on separate infrastructure, with signaling and media handled by different services, so that change shouldn't have reached it. The voice problems I remember came from client-side audio changes, not the backend rewrite. I could be wrong about the details, though, and I'd defer to anyone who worked on those systems directly.

Qwen 4 versus DeepSeek for coding work and self-hosting tradeoffs
I've been running both through a coding agent for the past couple of weeks. DeepSeek was more reliable on multi-file refactors. It kept track of existing function signatures and invented APIs less often. Qwen did better on short, well-specified tasks and on strict output formats. Hosted API pricing was close enough that I wouldn't decide on cost alone. If you plan to self-host, check the license terms and the quantized quality. Quantization changed my results more than the choice of base model did.

Raspberry Pi 6 pricing: no such model has been announced, so the Pi 5 is the current reference point.

As far as I know, there's no Raspberry Pi 6 released or officially announced, so there's no price to quote. The newest board is the Pi 5, which launched at $60 for the 4GB model and $80 for 8GB. If you're budgeting for a future model, I'd wait for an official announcement from the Raspberry Pi Foundation rather than trust leaks or retailer listings. Prices have also shifted with memory costs, so check current stock before you plan around any number.

Zed editor vs. Ghostty terminal: whether people are moving from one to the other, which are different kinds of tools

I don't think there's much switching, since they're in different categories. Zed is the editor and Ghostty is the terminal emulator, so the realistic comparison is Zed's built-in terminal panel versus running Ghostty next to whatever editor you already use. I moved my shell out of Zed's panel into Ghostty last month, mostly for better GPU rendering and font handling, but I kept Zed for editing. That's probably what most people who use both are doing.

Nintendo's legal pressure on the Project64 N64 emulator and how the project wound down.

I followed this one closely. Project64 was the big Windows N64 emulator, and in 2015 Nintendo sent a cease and desist. The team didn't fight it in court. They announced they were shutting the project down and pulled the official downloads, and the source was archived. Forks kept going, but the official site never came back. As far as I know there was no published court ruling. Nintendo usually sends letters to hosts and developers rather than suing, which is why these cases tend to end in a shutdown instead of a judgment.

Asahi Linux support for the M5 MacBook Pro, noting that it doesn't boot there yet and commenters expect M3-and-later work to lag behind M1 and M2.

Short answer: it doesn't run on M5 yet, and I wouldn't expect it soon. The Asahi team spent years reverse engineering M1 and M2, and newer chips have been slower to get working. Each generation changes the GPU, interrupt controller, and boot chain, so every chip is close to a new port. Most people I've seen discussing it say M1 and M2 machines are still the best choice for Linux, since they have the most complete GPU acceleration and battery support. I'd check the Asahi status page before assuming anything about a specific model.

Debian's systemd default init status: systemd has been the default since Debian 8 and is not being removed, though other init systems remain packaged.

No, not as far as I know. systemd has been Debian's default init since Jessie in 2015, after a general resolution vote in 2014. Other init systems like sysvinit and OpenRC are still packaged, so you can boot without systemd if you want. Devuan exists specifically to maintain a systemd-free fork of Debian. I run a few Debian boxes and haven't seen any plan to drop it. If you're worried about a specific change, the debian-devel list or the release notes for your target version are the places to confirm.

B200 idle power draw per GPU, measured with nvidia-smi on a 1000 W-TDP SXM part, with the driver and power state as variables
Our 8-GPU B200 nodes sat around 140 to 180 W per GPU at idle in nvidia-smi, well below the 1000 W TDP. Once a job touches the GPUs and clocks ramp up, draw climbs fast, so idle is a much smaller share than people assume. The exact floor depends on driver version, persistence mode, and any power limits you've set. I'd sample power.draw with nvidia-smi over several minutes rather than trust a spec sheet, since the idle number moved noticeably between driver releases for us.

OpenBSD's funded security code audit and what became of its findings

Honestly, I don't think there was ever a single published "audit report" to point to. The funded work was mostly people reading code and fixing bugs as they went, and the fixes landed as ordinary commits. Theo's style has always been to push fixes and skip the polished write-up. After the grant money ran down, the work kept going informally, with some people still doing audit passes on their own time. If you want the actual results, I'd check the commit logs from that period and the errata pages rather than look for a summary document.
